title: RC circuit charging: what the time constant tells you
examples: What is the time constant of an RC circuit?
How long does a capacitor take to charge?
Why does a capacitor charge exponentially?

explain.say: A camera flash whines for a few seconds before it is ready. That wait is a capacitor charging through a resistor. On the board, a 9 volt battery will charge a 100 microfarad capacitor through a 10 kilohm resistor. The switch is still open. Let's close it and watch the charge build up.

parts.label: C
parts.ask: Why does an empty capacitor act like a wire at first?

explain.say: The switch closes. At that very instant the capacitor is empty, so it has no voltage and behaves like a plain wire. All 9 volts sit across the resistor, and the current is 9 volts over 10 kilohms, 0.9 milliamps, the biggest it will ever be. As charge piles up on the capacitor, what happens to the voltage left for the resistor?

parts.label: R
parts.ask: What does the resistor do in an RC circuit?

parts.label: C
parts.ask: Why does an empty capacitor act like a wire at first?

explain.say: It shrinks, so the current slows down. That gives the curve on the board: the capacitor voltage rises quickly at first, then more and more gently, creeping towards 9 volts. The pace is set by the time constant, tau, equal to R times C: 10 kilohms times 100 microfarads is exactly 1 second. What fraction is reached after one tau?

curves.label: Resistor voltage
curves.ask: Why 63 percent after one time constant?

explain.say: About 63 percent, so 5.7 volts after 1 second. The resistor's voltage, the falling curve, does the mirror image, decaying from 9 volts. At every moment the two add up to 9 volts, which is Kirchhoff's voltage law at work. Where do the two curves cross?

explain.say: At 4.5 volts each, after about 0.69 seconds, which is tau times the natural log of 2. Fantastic! Rule of thumb: after 5 tau, here 5 seconds, the capacitor is over 99 percent full, so engineers call it charged. Defibrillators and flash units rely on exactly this. Challenge: what is tau with a 20 kilohm resistor?

faq.q: What is the time constant of an RC circuit?
faq.a: Tau equals R times C, in seconds. After one tau a charging capacitor reaches about 63 percent of its final voltage; after five tau it is practically full.

faq.q: Why does an empty capacitor act like a wire at first?
faq.a: An empty capacitor has no voltage across it, so at the first instant it does not oppose the current at all. As charge builds, its voltage rises and it pushes back.
asks: Why is the current biggest at t = 0 in an RC circuit?

faq.q: What does the resistor do in an RC circuit?
faq.a: It limits the charging current, and together with C it sets the time constant. A bigger resistor means a smaller current and slower charging.
asks: Why does a bigger R slow charging?

faq.q: Why 63 percent after one time constant?
faq.a: The capacitor voltage is the final voltage times 1 minus e to the minus t over tau. At t equals tau that is 1 minus 1 over e, about 0.632.
Closing it starts the charging at time zero. Opening it again stops the current, and an ideal capacitor would then hold its voltage.
asks: What happens when the switch opens?

facts: After five time constants a charging capacitor is within 1 percent of its final voltage.
One farad is one coulomb of charge stored per volt.

quiz.say: R is 47 kilohms and C is 10 microfarads. What is the time constant?
quiz.show: R = 47 kΩ and C = 10 µF. What is the time constant?
quiz.why: Tau is R times C: 47,000 times 0.00001, which is 0.47 seconds.

wrong.1: That is ten times too big; check the powers of ten.
wrong.2: That is ten times too small; 47 milliseconds is 0.047 seconds.

quiz.say: After one time constant, a charging capacitor has reached about what fraction of the supply voltage?
quiz.show: After one time constant, a charging capacitor has reached about what fraction of the supply voltage?
quiz.why: One minus 1 over e is about 0.632, so roughly 63 percent.

wrong.1: Half is reached a little earlier, at about 0.69 tau.
wrong.2: About 37 percent is what remains to go, or what a discharging capacitor keeps.
